marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q015.takeaway: Coracoid process is palpable immediately inferior to clavicle in deltopectoral region.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q015.displayText: The part of the scapula marked A is palpable in the infraclavicular fossa and is the coracoid process. The apex of the coracoid process lies approximately 2.5 cm below the clavicle, immediately lateral to the infraclavicular fossa (deltopectoral triangle), and can be palpated below the clavicle.

rationales.b: Label B is not the coracoid process; source image marks the palpable scapular landmark A.
rationales.c: Label C points elsewhere along scapula and is not the subclavicular coracoid tip.
rationales.d: Label D is not the coracoid process in the source image.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q016.takeaway: Pronation and supination occur at radioulnar and humeroradial articulations, not wrist.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q016.displayText: Pronation and supination do not occur at the radiocarpal (wrist) joint. These movements mainly occur at the humeroradial, superior radioulnar and inferior radioulnar joints. The middle radioulnar joint is a fibrous syndesmosis that binds radius and ulna and helps transmit weight from radius toward ulna.
emphasis: Pronation and supination do not occur at the radiocarpal (wrist) joint

rationales.a: Supination and pronation occur at superior radioulnar joint.
rationales.c: Distal radioulnar joint contributes to pronation/supination.
rationales.d: Humeroradial articulation also participates in forearm rotation; wrist is the exception.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q017.takeaway: Lateral epicondyle is outside elbow capsule and cannot be viewed arthroscopically from within.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q017.displayText: During intracapsular arthroscopy the lateral epicondyle cannot be seen because it is extracapsular. The elbow joint capsule is attached anteriorly just above the coronoid and radial fossae and posteriorly above the olecranon fossa. The source also notes that the medial epicondyle is extracapsular.

rationales.a: Coronoid fossa lies within the anterior capsule and can be seen arthroscopically.
rationales.b: Radial fossa is an anterior intracapsular depression.
rationales.c: Olecranon fossa is intracapsular posteriorly; lateral epicondyle is extracapsular.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q018.takeaway: Normal carrying angle averages about 17 degrees.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q018.displayText: The average carrying angle is approximately 17 degrees. It is the angle between the fully supinated forearm and the long axis of the humerus when the elbow is fully extended. It is usually about 10-15 degrees in males and more than 15 degrees in females, varies among individuals, and increases with age. Clinically, the contralateral side should be compared. The source notes that about 5-15 degrees is considered normal clinically; the carrying angle decreases in cubitus varus and increases in cubitus valgus.

rationales.a: Zero degrees would mean no carrying angle, unlike normal valgus alignment.
rationales.b: Twenty degrees exceeds the approximate average and can reflect individual variation.
rationales.d: Twenty-three degrees is greater than the cited mean of about 17 degrees.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q019.takeaway: Middle radioulnar articulation is fibrous syndesmosis.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q019.displayText: The middle radioulnar joint is a fibrous joint (syndesmosis). Radius and ulna are united by the proximal radioulnar joint, middle radioulnar joint, and distal radioulnar joint. Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot synovial joints involved in pronation and supination. The middle radioulnar joint is formed by the oblique cord and interosseous membrane as syndesmoses. The source also summarizes structural joint classes: fibrous (sutures, syndesmosis, gomphosis), cartilaginous (primary/synchondrosis and secondary/symphysis), and synovial (ball-and-socket, saddle, condylar/bicondylar, ellipsoid, hinge, pivot/trochoid and plane).

rationales.a: Proximal radioulnar joint is synovial pivot, not a plane synovial classification for middle joint.
rationales.b: Middle radioulnar joint is a syndesmosis rather than cartilaginous joint.
rationales.c: It is fibrous rather than secondary cartilaginous; the interosseous membrane binds radius and ulna.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q020.takeaway: Hook of hamate fracture can irritate nearby deep branch of ulnar nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q020.displayText: Tenderness in the shown hypothenar region with pain radiating to the ring and little finger is suggestive of a hook of hamate fracture. The pain distribution is related to the close proximity of the ulnar nerve, particularly its deep branch. The hamate is a cuneiform carpal bone with a hamulus (hook) projecting from the distal part of its rough palmar surface. The source also gives the carpal-bone mnemonic: She (Scaphoid) Looks (Lunate) Too (Triquetral) Pretty (Pisiform) - Try (Trapezium) To (Trapezoid) Catch (Capitate) Her (Hamate).

rationales.a: Triquetrum is a proximal-row carpal bone, not the hook-shaped palmar hamate.
rationales.b: Pisiform lies anterior to triquetrum and is not the hook-of-hamate landmark.
rationales.d: Trapezoid lies distal to scaphoid under index metacarpal; ulnar hand pain and paresthesia favor hook of hamate.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q021.takeaway: First metacarpal epiphysis is proximal at base, unlike other metacarpals.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q021.displayText: The epiphysis of the first metacarpal is at the base; all other metacarpals have their epiphysis at the head. The first metacarpal is the shortest and stoutest metacarpal. Its base has a convexoconcave articular surface for a saddle synovial joint with trapezium. The first metacarpal fracture at the base is called Bennett's fracture. The source radiograph also illustrates early ossification at about 2.5 years.
emphasis: epiphysis of the first metacarpal is at the base

rationales.b: First metacarpal epiphysis is at its base, not neck.
rationales.c: Other metacarpals typically have head epiphyses; first metacarpal is the exception at base.
rationales.d: The first metacarpal base is the common site for Bennett fracture; shaft is not its epiphyseal location.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q022.takeaway: Distal ulna is excluded from radiocarpal joint by articular disc.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q022.displayText: The distal end of the ulna does not take part in formation of the radiocarpal (wrist) joint. The wrist is a synovial, biaxial, ellipsoid joint formed by the distal radius, articular disc of triangular fibrocartilage, and scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum. In neutral position, only scaphoid and lunate are in contact with the radius and articular disc; triquetrum comes into apposition with the disc only in full adduction.

rationales.a: Scaphoid forms part of radiocarpal articulation.
rationales.b: Triquetrum articulates with articular disc and contributes to wrist joint.
rationales.c: Distal radius forms the proximal articular surface; distal ulna is separated from carpus by TFCC disc.
